https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8e.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Russian missiles and drones are hammering Ukraine's Black Sea ports, like Odesa By Paul Adams Diplomatic correspondent in Odesa Published 3 hours ago "My crane operator, my partner, died five metres from meâ¦ The driver remained in the cabin. He also died." Svitlana Halchenko winces as she remembers the Russian ballistic missile which exploded at work in Odesa, killing her colleagues. Svitlana works as a warehouse shift manager at the city's main port. Despite her injuries â she walks with a limp, pieces of shrapnel still embedded in her leg and back â Svitlana is determined to keep working. But her normally bustling workplace is largely silent. Russia is ramping up its efforts to strangle Ukraine's commercial links to the outside world, launching attacks all along the country's Black Sea coastline. From damaged port infrastructure to listing ships with bridges blackened and containers still smouldering, the evidence is everywhere. Nowhere more so than out towards the horizon, where the approaches to Ukraine's once bustling ports â Odesa, Chornomorsk, Pivdennyi â are almost devoid of ships. Svitlana maintains a brave smile throughout our conversation, but her distress is painfully obvious. Her fingers constantly twist a tissue as she tries to maintain her composure and she gazes into the distance as tears well up behind her glasses. The last few weeks have been worse than ever. "It's been very difficult for morale," she says with a deep sigh. "A lot of sirens, a lot of shaheds [drones], a lot of hits. People are very tense." Maarten Lernout/BBC My crane operator, my partner, died five metres from meâ¦ The driver remained in the cabin. He also died According to Ukraine's port administration, July saw 57 Russian attacks on civilian vessels, 22 of them at sea, and a further 67 hits on port infrastructure. While there have been Russian attacks on international vessels before, they've never been so numerous or so deadly. On July 19, a Turkish-owned cargo vessel, Golden Leo, was struck by three Russian missiles, killing nine Indian and Syrian crew members and a Ukrainian pilot. The ship, carrying Ukrainian corn, sank off Odesa a week later. According to the global shipping journal Lloyd's List, the Black Sea may now be the most dangerous place for shipping in the world - with July the deadliest month for merchant seamen , external since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. At his union's offices in the port city, Oleg Grygoriuk, Chairman of the Marine Transport Workers Union of Ukraine, says his members are suffering. "There are a lot of veterans who already served their country," he says, "and they literally say that being in the port is more scary than being on the front line." Odesa's proximity to Russian-occupied territory means that workers often have little time to react. "A missile flies from Crimea within a minute," he says. "If you are sitting in a crane, you need three and a half minutes to get down and go to the shelter. There's literally no time to do that." On a rare visit to one of the area's main ports, we saw almost no sign of movement. Hundreds of metres of berths sat empty and towering gantry cranes stood idle as a skeleton crew conducted maintenance. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Odesa's port lies empty now as Russia steps up its attacks The military authorities allowed the visit on strict condition that we neither name the facility nor film anything. Ukraine doesn't want Russia to know what has and hasn't been damaged or reveal details that might aid Moscow in further targeting. Two damaged cargo vessels were moored nearby. Both had suffered severe damage to the superstructure, where the bridge and crew quarters are located. Just one lone freighter was seen moving towards the port. "My heart is broken," a senior manager told us on condition we didn't name him. "Normally there's a queue, even out at sea, waiting for a berth." "There was a deal," he said, referring to the UN-brokered 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports. The agreement established safe maritime corridors to Odesa's main ports. "They stopped the deal in the middle of 2023, but they didn't start attacking it until recently," the manager said. "Today they do it systematically." Halfway through our tour, sirens sounded, forcing us to seek shelter for several minutes as a Russian jet-powered drone flew overhead. Weary dock workers scanned their phones for updates until the all-clear sounded. The manager said recent alerts have forced the port to shut down for 15 out of 24 hours. Technically, the port is open, as are all the others in the area. There is no prohibition on commercial ships attempting to use them. But the risks are clearly too great for most shipowners. "There is barely anybody who wants to call because there is a huge problem with people getting killed," says Andrey Stavnitser, co-owner and CEO of one of the largest ports in the area. "We can see that the whole supply chain is on hold." Image caption, Russia has made Ukraine's Black Sea coastline incredibly dangerous for shipping Stavnitser says Russia is almost certainly retaliating for Ukraine's recent, highly successful attacks on Russian shipping, including sanctioned vessels carrying oil, as well as other ships involved in ferrying supplies to Russian-occupied Crimea. Using its own drones, Ukraine's Operation MoLoChKa (which roughly translates as "Moscow will fall through Crimea") has struck around 200 Russian vessels, bringing traffic in the strategic Sea of Azov to a virtual standstill. Ukrainians bristle at the suggestion that Russia and Ukraine are playing the same game. Kyiv is attempting to loosen Moscow's grip on occupied territory, they point out, while Russia is preventing Ukraine from exporting badly needed grain to the international market. With Ukraine's summer grain harvest well under way, this is all happening at the worst possible time. "It's the most sensitive period," says Volodymyr Slavinskyi, trading director for Nibulon, one of the country's leading grain exporters. "Farmers need to quickly harvest grains from the fields, not to lose the crop. They need to be able to sell the crop they harvested and reinvest money in the next production cycle." The impact of a prolonged shutdown of Ukraine's ports are likely to be severe. Ukraine is one of the world's largest producers of grain and oilseeds, supplying around 6% of global wheat exports before Russia's full-scale invasion and 10% of corn exports. But reports suggest , external its export capacity has dropped by at least a third since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. The Black Sea remains a vital export route for the country. Last year, the Greater Odesa ports accounted for more than 73 million tonnes of Ukraine's maritime exports, with grain accounting for 38 million tonnes. With almost no vessels currently moving on Ukraine's Black Sea shipping corridor, traders are already counting the cost of this summer's closure. "I would say we've already lost the ability to deliver to global customers around half a million or 700,000 metric tons of Ukrainian grains and oilseeds," Slavinskyi says. Image source, Kristina Volk/BBC Image caption, Volodymyr Slavinskyi says Ukraine has lost a huge amount of its export capacity Away from the port, Odesa is determined to show off a very different side. The summer season is in full swing. The beaches are packed as visitors descend on the Black Sea from all over Ukraine. Buskers perform on the city's famous Potemkin Stairs, while sunbathers barely flinch as the sirens sound and explosions rumble in the distance. In a video published on Monday, swimmers were seen removing a Russian drone from the water as holidaymakers look on. They know the risks. In late June, 26-year-old Daria Kravchenko was killed when shrapnel from an intercepted Russian drone landed on the beach. This week, holidaymakers on Russia's equally Black Sea coast suffered a similar fate when an intercepted Ukrainian drone crashed onto a busy beach. Local authorities said seven people were killed, including three children. It's not clear what Ukraine was targeting, but this war on ships and ports has many casual victims. Sailors, dockworkers or people simply unlucky enough to live or work nearby. Outside Odesa, after a recent drone explosion, we found 83-year-old Andrii Dudik, surveying the mangled wreckage of his house and garden. He was physically unscathed and remarkably sanguine about the drone that had shattered his routine afternoon nap just hours earlier. "I was lying there, wondering what I was going to do this afternoon. Now I know," he joked. Did he feel like an accidental victim of Russia's attacks on the nearby ports, I asked him. "Absolutely," he replied. "And I won't forget it." (AP Photo/Vadim Ghirda, File) MIAMI – Prosecutors want social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate to remain in federal custody, arguing Monday that the brothers are a flight risk and a danger to the community, as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking. Three days after defense attorneys filed a motion for release, prosecutors filed their response in Miami federal court, where a hearing on Thursday will determine if the brothers should stay in jail or be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process. Recommended Videos The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. The detention hearing is likely to be the first time the Tates leave the Federal Detention Center in Miami since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest . The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in the Tates' long-running international legal saga spanning the U.S., Britain and Romania. Prosecutors claim a ‘heightened risk of flight’ According to the U.S. Attorney's Office filing, the Tates should be detained pending their extradition hearing because they cannot overcome the strong presumption against bail in international extradition cases. The serious pending U.K. charges involving human trafficking and violent rapes and assaults against multiple victims, along with allegations in Romania that the Tates attempted to intimidate witnesses , present a clear public safety concern, prosecutors say. “That the Tates also claim to maintain multiple passports and identities, have access to excessive wealth and influence in numerous countries, and are stridently unwilling to voluntarily return to face prosecution in the United Kingdom, collectively demonstrate a heightened risk of flight that no amount of bond could overcome,” the filing says. The defense motion filed Friday acknowledges there is a presumption against bond in extradition proceedings but argues that release can be granted in special circumstances. It says the Tates’ high profile makes it nearly impossible for them to flee, and that they regularly post updates about their locations on social media. While prosecutors call the brothers a flight risk, their attorneys said they have proved they are not by complying with all pretrial restrictions in Romania, where they are accused of luring women for sexual exploitation. The U.K. has until mid-September to provide evidence to the State Department to support extradition, meaning the brothers could spend months in FDC Miami before the proceedings are resolved, the defense motion says. No date has been set for an extradition hearing. They are being held in a special unit for their own protection. Legal troubles follow the Tate brothers The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn't expect any help from the president. British prosecutors said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in southeastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn't moved forward due to legal and procedural problems. The Tates' attorneys have said the Romanian court has granted a U.K. request for extradition that will take effect after Romanian proceedings conclude. Andrew Tate, 39, became famous a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was ejected from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. Tristan Tate, 38, has worked with his brother on multiple businesses, including the production of online webcam pornography. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. https://www.dw.com/en/ethiopia-s-militar.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NEYP Wrecked materiel litters the Tigray Region from several previous wars [FILE: June 20, 2021] Image: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images Advertisement Fighting between Ethiopian troops and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated on Thursday, threatening to shatter a fragile 2022 peace deal . The renewed fighting first broke out in the Tigray Region in northern Ethiopia on Wednesday. "We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice president Amanuel Assefa told AFP news agency. On Thursday, Ethiopia's military said it "launched a counter-offensive that inflicted heavy personnel and equipment losses on the TPLF." The military said it killed 272 people among the Tigrayan rebels and wounded some 260 more. These figures could not be independently verified, and there was no breakdown given for soldiers and civilians. Calls for deescelation The African Union , the United Nations and other international observers have called for restraint and deescelation. "I am disappointed to see the leadership of the TPLF, that the United States sanctioned earlier this year, make the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive today," said Ervin J. Massinga, the US ambassador in Addis Ababa. "Rejecting dialogue sponsored by the African Union under President Obasanjo and engaging in an unwinnable fight does nothing for the people," he added. TPLF troops patrolled the regional capital Mekele on Wednesday Image: AFP What led to the resumption in fighting? The TPLF was Ethiopia's dominant political force from 1991 until 2018. It governed with a coalition of other ethnic-based parties, but critics accused it of creating these parties as loyal opposition to sideline preexisting ethnic movements. When Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018, he sidelined the TPFL in favor of a government not based on ethnic lines, dominated by his Prosperity Party . Abiy's early foreign policy saw him repair relations with Ethiopia's former archrival Eritrea — efforts for which he was awarded the Noble Peace Prize in 2019. But his later determination for landlocked Ethiopia to have access to a seaport was seen as provocative in Eritrea as well in Somalia . Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The TPLF then launched a rebellion against Abiy in 2020, spiraling into a two-year war that saw some 500,000 killed due to violence, famine and the collapse of health services. During that war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie Amde decried "the forces of destruction and mayhem" and "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements." Ethiopia's President Taye Atske Selassie Amde condemned the brewing conflict at the UN General Assembly Image: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance Conflict spreads to Amhara region Fighting was also reported in the Amhara region in the Ethiopian highlands. The AFP news agency received reports of fighting around the holy city of Lalibela , home to Ethiopia's ancient, UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches. Flights to the popular tourist destination were suspended on Thursday. Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The TPLF announced an alliance with Amhara's Fano militia , a former foe that has been waging its own insurgency in the region since 2023. The Fano militia originally emerged as an opponent of TPFL rule and the two sides still have competing claims over land that was absorbed in to the Amhara region from the Tigray region after the last war. "The only issue joining them is their opposition to Prosperity Party rule," said Kjetil Tronvoll, a professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New ⁠University College. https://www.miragenews.com/opcw-chief-me.text: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News World 16 Oct 2026 10:54 pm AEDT Date Time Share The Director-General of the OPCW, Sabrina Dallafior, met Poland's Deputy Prime Minister/Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr Radosław Sikorski, at OPCW Headquarters in The Hague on 16 October 2026. Director-General Dallafior briefed the Deputy Prime Minister/Foreign Minister on her recent visit to Syria and highlighted the progress made in locating and destroying the remnants of the Assad-era chemical weapons programme. They also discussed the Technical Secretariat provisions of technical expertise in support of Ukraine's national investigation into the presence of the riot control agent CS along the confrontation lines. The Chemical Weapons Convention bans the use of riot control agents in warfare. Director-General Dallafior recognised Poland's continued support for the OPCW's mission, including through contributions to the Trust Fund for Syria Missions and leading negotiations on the annual resolution on the implementation of the Chemical Weapons Convention in the UN General Assembly. Deputy Prime Minister/Foreign Minister Sikorski stated that the "prohibition of chemical weapons use applies to all states, without exception. The experience of Syria and reports of Russia's use of chemical weapons against Ukraine demonstrate the critical importance of effective monitoring and enforcement of international obligations. Poland remains firmly committed to supporting the OPCW and its mission. The world must not allow the use of chemical weapons to become normalised." Background Poland signed the Chemical Weapons Convention on 13 January 1993, ratified it on 23 August 1995, and has been an OPCW Member State since the Convention entered into force on 29 April 1997. Poland has consistently supported OPCW activities concerning Ukraine and Syria. It has contributed to the OPCW Trust Fund for the Implementation of Article X and the Trust Fund for Syria Missions. /Public Release.
